text: Comparisons are the heart of decision-making, and every one of them produces a simple True or False.
Less-than, double-equals for equality, and exclamation-equals for not-equal — the basic building blocks.
[chuckle] You can combine several conditions with and and or, [sniff] and flip any result with not.
And needs both sides true, or needs only one side true, and not simply reverses whatever it's given.
Now here's something Python does that surprises newcomers — truthiness.
Certain values count as falsy even though they aren't literally False — zero, an empty string, an empty list.
[groan] And any value with actual content is truthy — a non-empty string, a list with items inside.
That lets you write clean checks like just 'if my_list' instead of comparing its length to zero.
One last subtlety: and and or short-circuit — if the left side of an and is already False, Python never even runs the right side.
